title: Oldowan stone tools
summary: By about 2.6 million years ago, early humans in east Africa were making simple stone tools from chipped pebbles and flakes. They are called Oldowan tools because the first such artefacts came from Olduvai Gorge. The Natural History Museum dates this type of tool from about 3.0 to 1.3 million years ago and calls it a significant shift in the technology available to early humans.

uncertainty.note: Begins with the earliest flaked stone tool assemblages at Gona and across East Africa by 2.6 Ma and persists until Acheulean handaxes supersede it around 1.7–1.5 Ma.

as_recorded.value: The earliest stone toolmaking developed by at least 2.6 million years ago

where.modern_name: Olduvai Gorge, Ngorongoro Conservation Area, Tanzania (eponymous type site for the Oldowan; earliest assemblages appear across East Africa)
where.historical_name: Paleolake basin and savanna margins, East African Rift; no human polities existed

importance.justification: The inception of systematic flaked stone tool technology, fundamentally transforming hominin dietary access to meat and marrow and inaugurating the archaeological record.

related.because: Habitual bipedal locomotion freed early hominin hands for precise percussive manipulation and stone knapping.
